cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{PPAD}=\mathrm{FP}\), where FP means polynomial-time solvability of total search problems? Equivalently, does one uniform deterministic algorithm solve every End-of-Line instance in time polynomial in its complete circuit encoding length? End-of-Line is the directed-path search task specified below by two Boolean circuits, including the exact answer condition at the distinguished zero vertex. The algorithm receives the full circuit descriptions and has no oracle.
cards.definitions:
A Boolean circuit is given explicitly by a topologically ordered list of gates over fan-in-two AND and OR, unary NOT, and constants 0 and 1, together with a list of input nodes and an ordered list of output nodes. Gate types, wire indices, counts, and list delimiters are written in an unambiguous binary encoding; the full lists, rather than a program generating them, are part of the input. The number of listed inputs and outputs is included in the encoding length. Each circuit in this card has \(n\ge1\) input bits and \(n\) output bits. The symbol \(0^n\) denotes the all-zero string of length \(n\).

An End-of-Line input consists of two such circuits \(S,P:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^n\). It is valid when \(P(0^n)=0^n\) and \(S(0^n)\ne0^n\), two conditions checked by evaluating the circuits. An accepted answer is a string \(v\in\{0,1\}^n\) satisfying
\[P(S(v))\ne v\quad\text{or}\quad\bigl(v\ne0^n\ \text{and}\ S(P(v))\ne v\bigr).\]
Thus \(v=0^n\) is allowed only for the first condition: it is not accepted merely for being the designated start. If either input condition fails, the only accepted answer is INVALID. No promise that \(P\) and \(S\) are global inverses is imposed. The intended graph has an edge from \(u\) to \(v\) when \(u\ne v\), \(S(u)=v\), and \(P(v)=u\); the displayed circuit condition, rather than an informal drawing, defines every accepted answer. The task accepts any answer meeting that condition, with no requirement that it be reachable from \(0^n\).

Let \(N\) be the complete input bit length. Polynomial time means that there exist one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine and integers \(a,d\ge1\), independent of \(n\) and all circuits, such that the machine halts within \(a(N+1)^d\) steps on every input encoding. Every bit operation and output bit is charged. The machine receives the gate lists themselves and may inspect them; it has no advice, randomness, or oracle. On a malformed encoding it must return a distinguished INVALID symbol; that symbol is forbidden on valid instances.

A total NP search problem is a relation \(R(x,y)\) on finite bit strings for which valid answers \(y\) have length bounded by a fixed polynomial in \(|x|\), validity is decidable in deterministic polynomial time, and at least one valid answer exists for every input \(x\). The class of these problems is TFNP. A deterministic polynomial-time many-one search reduction from \(R\) to \(Q\) consists of maps \(f,g\), computable in polynomial time, such that every valid \(Q\)-answer \(z\) on \(f(x)\) gives the valid \(R\)-answer \(g(x,z)\). Here FP denotes the subclass of total search problems with a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm selecting a valid answer, not a requirement that the relation have a unique answer.

PPAD is the subclass of TFNP whose problems admit the many-one search reduction just defined to End-of-Line. Consequently polynomial-time solvability of End-of-Line is equivalent to polynomial-time solvability of every PPAD problem. The explicit INVALID convention only handles efficiently detectable malformed instances and does not impose a new promise-recognition problem.

context_blocks.text: A directed path has two ends. If a finite graph gives every vertex at most one predecessor and one successor, knowing one start guarantees another endpoint somewhere in the graph. Here exponentially many possible vertices are described by short circuits, so the existence of another endpoint does not itself provide a polynomial-time method to find it.

PPAD abbreviates Polynomial Parity Argument, Directed. It collects total search problems reducible to this circuit endpoint problem. FP denotes the total search problems admitting polynomial-time solution algorithms; both conventions are specified precisely in Definitions. Papadimitriou explicitly posed the tractability question in the 1994 paper's list of open problems.

In a mixed Nash equilibrium, players randomize independently over their actions and no player can improve expected payoff by changing only their own strategy. Chen, Deng and Teng proved that finding such an equilibrium in an explicitly listed rational two-player game is PPAD-complete. Completeness transfers the polynomial-time tractability question; it is not an unconditional proof that equilibrium computation is hard.

The continuous-local-search class CLS is the intersection of PPAD and PLS, where PLS represents potential-based local search. Accordingly, an affirmative answer here would also settle CLS versus FP affirmatively, but the converse is not known. The existing TCS500 benchmark question about coordination-only polymatrix games concerns a restricted equilibrium problem, whereas this card addresses the entire PPAD class.

The input model matters. A lower bound for algorithms that can only query a hidden graph or a hidden function does not exclude an algorithm exploiting an explicit circuit's description. The November 2026 random-oracle preprint studies circuits with access to an additional random function. Its announced separations concern that oracle model, so they do not settle this ordinary, oracle-free question.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that one uniform deterministic algorithm always returns a valid answer within a fixed polynomial in the full input bit length, or prove that no such algorithm exists. The theorem must cover the exact End-of-Line relation, including malformed inputs and the zero-vertex convention. A separation relative to an oracle, a query lower bound, conditional cryptographic hardness, a randomized solver alone, or a guarantee restricted to special circuits does not settle this target. This card requests the unconditional yes/no answer, not a specific polynomial exponent.

cards.title: Additive-error exponent of linear-size spanners
cards.formal: For every fixed real edge-budget coefficient \(c\ge1\), determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the exponent \[x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)=\inf\{a\ge0:A_c(n)+1=O_c(n^a)\text{ as }n\to\infty\}.\] Here \(A_c(n)\), defined below, is the largest, over simple undirected unweighted \(n\)-vertex graphs, minimum additive all-pairs distance error of a spanning subgraph with at most \(\lfloor cn\rfloor\) edges and the same connected components. The edge budget is genuinely linear; no hidden logarithmic factor in the budget is allowed.
cards.why: The linear edge regime compresses a graph to a constant number of retained edges per vertex. Determining its unavoidable distance loss would quantify a fundamental limit on how accurately arbitrary graph metrics can survive such strong sparsification.
cards.status_note: The survey leaves the linear-size error tradeoff open. The later lower-bound and nearly linear upper-bound abstracts were checked on 13 September 2026 and do not give matching bounds for every fixed linear coefficient. cards.definitions: For every \(n\geq1\), let \(\mathcal G_n\) be the finite set of simple undirected graphs on \([n]\). Every edge has length one. A spanning subgraph \(H\subseteq G\) has the same vertices, retains only original edges, and must have the same connected components as \(G\). There are no Steiner vertices, shortcut edges or changed edge lengths. Let \[\Delta(G,H)=\max_{u,v:\,d_G(u,v)<\infty}\bigl(d_H(u,v)-d_G(u,v)\bigr),\qquad A_c(n)=\max_{G\in\mathcal G_n}\min_{\substack{H\subseteq G,\ |E(H)|\leq\lfloor cn\rfloor\\ H\text{ preserves components}}}\Delta(G,H).\] Distances count edges. Pairs with \(u=v\) are included, so the maximum is defined and nonnegative even in an edgeless graph. A spanning forest is feasible for \(c\geq1\); thus the quantity is finite. This measures optimal structural approximation, not the running time for finding a spanner; no algorithmic cost bound is imposed. The explicit coefficient \(c\) makes the source’s unspecified linear-size constant a parameter of the target. Define the exponent \[x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \exists n_0\ge1\ \forall n\ge n_0,\ A_c(n)+1\le Cn^a\}.\] For each fixed real \(c\ge1\), the constants may depend on \(c\) and \(a\), but not on the graph or \(n\). Adding one removes zero-value conventions without changing any positive power of growth. A spanning forest has finite distances at most \(n-1\) within its components, so \(0\le x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)\le1\). The infimum need not be attained; no ordinary logarithmic-growth limit is assumed. In particular, exponent zero permits polylogarithmic or other subpolynomial error and does not promise bounded error.

context_blocks.text: The survey’s Section 8.4, item 3, asks how much additive error is unavoidable with \(O(n)\) retained edges. Its dated bounds leave a polynomial gap between what sparse subgraphs can achieve and what some input metrics force.

Bodwin and Hoppenworth subsequently establish an \(\Omega(n^{1/7})\) additive-error lower bound for linear-size spanners, improving the lower bound quoted in the survey. This is a lower bound, not a matching determination.

The later Almost-Optimal Sublinear Additive Spanners abstract reports \(O(n^{0.403})\) additive error with \(\widetilde O(n)\) edges. That edge budget hides logarithmic factors and cannot be substituted for a fixed \(cn\) budget in this question.

cards.answer_criterion: Supply one explicitly described real-valued function \(a\) on all real \(c\ge1\). Prove in Lean that \(|a(c)-x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)|\le1/100\) at every point of that domain. A pair of [certified bounding functions](definitions.html#numerical-answers) \(L,U\) also qualifies if \(L(c)\le x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)\le U(c)\) and \(U(c)-L(c)\le1/50\) everywhere, with \(a=(L+U)/2\). Use the same edge budget \(\lfloor cn\rfloor\) on both sides.

cards.title: A dichotomy for edge deletion with finitely many forbidden induced subgraphs
cards.formal: For every fixed finite family \(\mathcal F\) of finite simple undirected graphs, is the following decision problem either in \(\mathrm{P}\) or \(\mathrm{NP}\)-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions? Given a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) and integer \(k\geq0\), decide whether there is \(S\subseteq E\) with \(|S|\leq k\) such that \(G-S\) has no induced subgraph isomorphic to any member of \(\mathcal F\).
cards.why: Edge deletion is a basic graph-repair operation whose tractability changes with the desired hereditary property. A dichotomy for every finite forbidden list would explain this variation across many graph classes and locate a general boundary between efficient repair and NP-completeness.

cards.definitions: A simple undirected graph has no loops or parallel edges. For \(U\subseteq V\), its induced subgraph contains every edge of \(G\) with both endpoints in \(U\). Graph isomorphism is an adjacency-preserving bijection of vertex sets. The class of \(\mathcal F\)-free graphs consists of all finite graphs with none of the forbidden induced subgraphs; it is hereditary, meaning closed under taking induced subgraphs. Deleting \(S\) retains all vertices and exactly the edges in \(E\setminus S\). Edges cannot be added, vertices cannot be removed, and every deleted edge costs one. The empty graph and the empty forbidden family are permitted. The input graph uses its adjacency matrix on numbered vertices; \(k\) is binary. The family \(\mathcal F\) is fixed before the input varies and is not part of the input to this decision problem. For each fixed family, its finite graph list may be built into the program, and polynomial exponents and constants may depend on it. A language is in \(\mathrm{P}\) if a deterministic Turing machine decides it in polynomial input length. It is in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if polynomial-size certificates can be checked in polynomial time. A polynomial-time many-one reduction from \(K\) to \(L\) is one deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) on finite binary strings such that \(x\in K\) iff \(f(x)\in L\). NP-completeness means membership in NP and such a reduction from every NP language. Each problem here is in NP because a deletion set can be checked and all induced copies of the finitely many fixed forbidden graphs can be enumerated in polynomial time. The dichotomy is inclusive; it assumes neither \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) nor its negation.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every finite family \(\mathcal F\) satisfies the stated P-or-NP-complete alternative. Alternatively specify one finite family and prove in Lean that its decision problem is neither in P nor NP-complete under the stated reductions. A theorem for a single forbidden graph or a fixed selection of graph classes is insufficient. No separate effective procedure for classifying the family \(\mathcal F\) is imposed by this proposition.

context_blocks.text: The survey describes the absence of a general polynomial-time versus NP-hard classification for hereditary edge deletion. Editorial specialization: this card selects the finite-forbidden-induced-subgraph domain, giving the graph properties a finite description and ensuring that every resulting decision problem is in NP. The source’s broader direction also encompasses hereditary classes without such a finite forbidden list.

There are immediate tractable families. If the only forbidden graph is a single edge, all input edges must be removed. If the forbidden graphs are the three-vertex path and the triangle, every remaining component must be an isolated vertex or an isolated edge: maximizing the retained edges is maximum matching, which is polynomial-time solvable.

Deleting an edge can create a forbidden induced subgraph. For example, removing one edge from a triangle creates an induced three-vertex path. Consequently, eliminating all forbidden copies initially visible in the input need not produce a valid final graph.

The survey contrasts edge deletion with the classical broad hardness theorem for vertex removal into nontrivial hereditary properties. That contrast motivates a structural classification for edge operations; it does not transfer the vertex-removal theorem to the problem defined here.

The 2023 journal version still states the absence of a general edge-removal dichotomy. Its detailed tables also concern parameterized algorithms and kernelization. A bound depending arbitrarily on the deletion budget, or the existence of a polynomial kernel, addresses a different question from ordinary polynomial time in the entire input.

Completing the dichotomy would rule out NP-intermediate behavior inside this finite-description family, even if such behavior exists elsewhere in NP. Proving just that some cases are hard is weaker: every finite forbidden family must fall into one of the stated alternatives.

cards.context:
The survey describes the absence of a general polynomial-time versus NP-hard classification for hereditary edge deletion. Editorial specialization: this card selects the finite-forbidden-induced-subgraph domain, giving the graph properties a finite description and ensuring that every resulting decision problem is in NP. The source’s broader direction also encompasses hereditary classes without such a finite forbidden list.

There are immediate tractable families. If the only forbidden graph is a single edge, all input edges must be removed. If the forbidden graphs are the three-vertex path and the triangle, every remaining component must be an isolated vertex or an isolated edge: maximizing the retained edges is maximum matching, which is polynomial-time solvable.

Deleting an edge can create a forbidden induced subgraph. For example, removing one edge from a triangle creates an induced three-vertex path. Consequently, eliminating all forbidden copies initially visible in the input need not produce a valid final graph.

The survey contrasts edge deletion with the classical broad hardness theorem for vertex removal into nontrivial hereditary properties. That contrast motivates a structural classification for edge operations; it does not transfer the vertex-removal theorem to the problem defined here.

The 2023 journal version still states the absence of a general edge-removal dichotomy. Its detailed tables also concern parameterized algorithms and kernelization. A bound depending arbitrarily on the deletion budget, or the existence of a polynomial kernel, addresses a different question from ordinary polynomial time in the entire input.

Completing the dichotomy would rule out NP-intermediate behavior inside this finite-description family, even if such behavior exists elsewhere in NP. Proving just that some cases are hard is weaker: every finite forbidden family must fall into one of the stated alternatives.

cards.title: NP membership of word-equation satisfiability
cards.formal:
Let \(\mathrm{WE}\) be the language of encodings of satisfiable word equations \(u=v\) over finite free monoids, as defined below. Is
\[
\mathrm{WE}\in\mathrm{NP}?
\]
Explicitly, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(V\), a constant \(C\ge1\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that \(V\) halts on every pair of bit strings \((e,w)\) within \(C(|e|+|w|+1)^k\) steps and, for every valid equation encoding \(e\) of length \(N\),
\[
e\in\mathrm{WE}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{*}\ 
\bigl(|w|\le C(N+1)^k\ \text{and}\ V(e,w)=1\bigr)?
\]
The verifier rejects invalid equation encodings. The same machine and constants work for all alphabets, equations and variable sets.
cards.why: Word equations are a basic model of string constraints and associative unification. Their decidability is established, but the gap between NP-hardness and polynomial-space algorithms leaves the complexity of short verifiable evidence unresolved. NP membership would place the unrestricted satisfiability problem at the familiar NP-complete boundary.

cards.definitions:
For an integer \(a\ge1\), the constant alphabet is \(\Sigma=\{a_1,\ldots,a_a\}\). Its free monoid \(\Sigma^*\) is the set of finite words, including the empty word \(\varepsilon\), with concatenation as the operation. Concatenation is associative and \(\varepsilon\) is its identity; distinct letters do not commute by assumption.

The variable set is \(\mathcal X=\{X_1,\ldots,X_r\}\), disjoint from \(\Sigma\), where \(r\ge0\). An equation is a pair \(u,v\in(\Sigma\cup\mathcal X)^*\). Both sides are explicitly written token sequences. A solution assigns one word \(\sigma(X_i)\in\Sigma^*\) to each variable, fixes every constant letter, and extends by concatenation. The equation is satisfiable exactly when \(\sigma(u)=\sigma(v)\) for some assignment. All occurrences of a variable receive the same word. Empty words, repeated variables, variables on both sides, and equations with empty sides are allowed. There are no length constraints, regular-language restrictions, inverse symbols or inequalities.

One precise binary encoding is as follows. Write \(1^a0\,1^r0\,1^{\ell_u}0\,1^{\ell_v}0\), where \(\ell_u=|u|\) and \(\ell_v=|v|\) count tokens. Follow this header by all tokens of \(u\) and then all tokens of \(v\). Each token is encoded in \(b=\lceil\log_2(a+r+1)\rceil\) bits: code \(i\) for \(a_i\) and code \(a+j\) for \(X_j\). Codes outside \(1,\ldots,a+r\) are invalid. There must be exactly \(\ell_u+\ell_v\) token blocks and no trailing data. Thus
\[
N=a+r+\ell_u+\ell_v+4+b(\ell_u+\ell_v).
\]
This explicit encoding fixes bit complexity without allowing compressed input equations.

Use [NP](definitions.html#p-np), with precisely the soundness and completeness quantified above. A certificate is any finite binary string. It need not contain the substituted words explicitly, and no particular compressed representation is prescribed. A satisfiable input must have some short accepting certificate; an unsatisfiable input must have none.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of \(\mathrm{WE}\in\mathrm{NP}\). A positive answer must specify the verifier and prove the polynomial time and certificate bounds together with soundness and completeness for every input. A negative answer must prove that no such verifier exists; failure of one certificate format or long explicit solutions is insufficient. This binary target has no numerical \(1/100\) tolerance. Results only for boundedly many variables, bounded occurrences, or added constraints do not decide the full statement.

cards.definitions: Use atoms \(p_{i}\) and their distinct dual literals \(p_{i}^{\perp}\) for integers \(i\ge 0\). Formulas are finite syntax trees generated by \(A ::= p_{i} | p_{i}^{\perp} | 1 | \perp  | (A\otimes A) |\) (A⅋A) | !A | ?A. A sequent \(\Gamma\) is a finite multiset of formulas; commas denote multiset union, retaining multiplicity. The following rules, read from premises to conclusion, define derivations. Identity has no premises and concludes \(\vdash p_{i},p_{i}^{\perp}\). The unit rule has no premises and concludes \(\vdash 1\). Tensor takes \(\vdash \Gamma ,A\) and \(\vdash \Delta ,B\) to \(\vdash \Gamma ,\Delta ,A\otimes B\). Par takes \(\vdash \Gamma ,A,B\) to \(\vdash \Gamma ,A\)⅋B. The other unit rule takes \(\vdash \Gamma\) to \(\vdash \Gamma ,\perp\). Dereliction takes \(\vdash \Gamma ,A\) to \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A. Weakening takes \(\vdash \Gamma\) to \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A. Contraction takes \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A,?A to \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A. Promotion takes \(\vdash\)?\(\Gamma ,A\) to \(\vdash\)?\(\Gamma ,!A\), where every formula in ?\(\Gamma\) has outermost symbol ?. Contexts may be empty, and all displayed formula and context choices are arbitrary subject to these conditions. A derivation is a finite rooted tree whose leaves are the two nullary rules and whose internal nodes are instances of the other rules. There are no further rules; exchange is implicit in multisets. This is the cut-free presentation of classical commutative MELL, whose usual cut rule is admissible. Inputs explicitly list formula trees with constructor delimiters and binary atom indices; malformed strings are rejected. Formulas contain neither additives nor quantifiers, and there is just one pair of exponential modalities ! and ?.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the provable sequents of this calculus form a decidable language, or prove that no algorithm can decide that language. A procedure that terminates only on provable sequents does not establish decidability.

context_blocks.text: Linear logic treats assumptions as resources whose occurrences matter. An ordinary assumption cannot automatically be copied or discarded. For example, the resource-reading of \(p\to p\otimes p\) asks for two copies from one and is unavailable in general; marking the input !p permits reuse. MELL keeps multiplicative composition together with these reuse modalities.

The rules make each proposed finite proof checkable. That does not by itself make provability decidable: searching through larger proofs will eventually find a proof when one exists, but need not terminate when none exists. The question asks for a single procedure that also gives a terminating negative answer.

The restrictions on contraction and promotion are part of the problem. Allowing unrestricted contraction gives a different logic, and adding additive connectives or several interacting subexponential modalities changes the decidability boundary. A published 2015 decidability argument was challenged in Straßburger’s 2019 paper, which identifies gaps and separates MELL from its decidable relevant variant.

Branching vector addition systems describe trees of computations with nonnegative integer resources. Their general reachability problem is inter-reducible with MELL provability. The 2025 result in the original reference establishes decidability for two-dimensional systems, so its dimension restriction cannot be omitted.

Status update: the July 2026 preprint claims decidability of general branching vector addition systems and explicitly states that MELL provability follows. This reaches the full decision question, unlike the earlier low-dimensional result. This card records the claim with uncertain status because its proof has not been independently verified here.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic-space streaming Euclidean MST estimation
cards.formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized one-pass insertion-only streaming algorithm A and absolute constants \(C\ge1\), \(K\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), \(d\ge1\), \(\Delta\ge2\), and every stream of n distinct points in \(\{0,\ldots,\Delta\}^{d}\), A uses at most
\[K\bigl(d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\lceil\log_2(\Delta+2)\rceil\bigr)^k\]
bits of working memory and returns a rational estimate Z satisfying
\[\Pr[\operatorname{MST}(X)\le Z\le C\operatorname{MST}(X)]\ge 2/3?\]
The stream order is arbitrary and fixed independently of the algorithm’s private random bits. The output estimates total Euclidean MST cost; it need not describe a tree. For polynomially bounded integer coordinates, the required space is \(\mathrm{poly}(d\log n)\), as in the community proposal.
cards.definitions:
The point set X consists of the n distinct inserted vectors. Coordinates are nonnegative integers given in binary, and the parameters n,d and the bound \(\Delta\) are supplied before the stream. The graph is complete on X; an edge between x and y has weight \(\|x-y\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^{d}(x_j-y_j)^2)^{1/2}\). The quantity \(\operatorname{MST}(X)\) is the minimum sum of edge weights over all spanning trees of this graph. It is a real number even though the input coordinates are integers.

The algorithm is one fixed finite probabilistic Turing-machine program with a read-once input stream, private independent fair random bits, working tapes, and an output tape used only for the final rational estimate. An input record may be buffered, with those bits charged to memory. All retained state, counters, random seeds and postprocessing workspace count toward the space bound, on every input and every random tape. Consumed input cannot be revisited, and there are no deletions, extra passes, random-order promise, external storage, nonuniform advice or real-number registers. The machine must halt on every random tape; no separate update-time or total-time bound is imposed. The probability is over its coins for each fixed stream. The constants and exponent do not depend on n,d or the coordinate bound.

Dependence polynomial in the bit length of coordinates makes the finite-input convention explicit. In particular, for each fixed integer b and \(\Delta\le n^b\), the bound has the proposal’s \(\mathrm{poly}(d\log n)\) form. The logarithmic coordinate factor is recorded rather than silently treating arbitrary reals as constant-size words. The target allows d to grow, including \(d=\Theta(\log n)\); a bound exponential in d does not qualify. The approximation constant can be any fixed finite C. Requiring the estimate to lie above the true cost is a normalization: a two-sided constant-factor estimate can be rescaled at the cost of changing C. Neither an explicit tree nor a \(1+\varepsilon\) approximation is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm satisfying the stated memory, pass and probability bounds for some absolute finite approximation constant, or prove the negation for every such algorithm and constants. An \(n^{\varepsilon}\)-space algorithm for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), a factor growing with n, a multiple-pass algorithm, or a lower bound excluding only constants near 1 does not settle this target.
cards.why: An MST measures the cost of connecting an entire geometric data set. A small summary that estimates this global quantity within a constant factor would clarify how much connectivity information survives a single streaming pass as dimension grows.

cards.title: Nearly quadratic oracle complexity for convex-body volume
cards.formal: Is there a randomized classical membership-oracle algorithm such that, for every fixed \(a\ge1\), every \(n\ge2\), and every convex body \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) with \(B_2^n\subseteq K\subseteq n^a B_2^n\), it returns \(V\) satisfying \[\Pr[|V-\operatorname{vol}_n(K)|\le\operatorname{vol}_n(K)/10]\ge2/3\] using at most \(C_a n^2(\log(2+n))^{c_a}\) membership queries in expectation? The polynomial-radius promise and origin are supplied; no isotropic position or uniform-sampling oracle is given.
cards.definitions:
A convex body is a compact convex set with nonempty interior, and \(B_2^n=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_2\le1\}\). Volume means n-dimensional Lebesgue measure. More generally, supplied concentric radii \(r,R\) and center \(z\), with \(R/r\le n^a\), can be rescaled to this normalization; volume scales by \(r^n\). The exponent \(a\) is fixed independently of dimension, and the constants may depend on it.

The only access to the unknown body is the exact bit indicating whether a queried real point belongs to \(K\), including its boundary. Queries can be adaptive and randomized. The information model permits measurable choices of exact real points and arbitrary measurable computation between queries, all of which are uncharged. Every membership answer costs one query. No separation, optimization, boundary, quantum-superposition or conditional-sampling oracle is available. Randomness belongs to the algorithm; the body itself is adversarially fixed.

The algorithm must terminate almost surely. Both its expected query bound and success guarantee hold for each eligible body. An expected bound is the selected interpretation of oracle complexity, rather than a bound on every random tape. Preprocessing, rounding and production of auxiliary samples must pay for all membership queries they use. In particular, one cannot assume an isotropic transformation has already been found for free.

The relative accuracy \(1/10\) and probability \(2/3\) are fixed constants in the computational task. The TCS500 benchmark's absolute \(1/100\) rule for numerical answers does not replace this algorithmic success condition. The target bounds information from the oracle, not total arithmetic operations or the bit length needed to represent continuously distributed query points.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of an algorithm with the stated uniform relative-accuracy and expected-query guarantees, or its negation in the classical query model. A bound assuming free isotropic rounding, a quantum algorithm, or an estimate for a constant-dimensional high-precision regime does not suffice. A matching-order lower bound alone does not prove the requested upper bound.

cards.title: Planar k-set growth exponent
cards.formal: Determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the exponent \[x_{\mathrm{kset}}=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall 1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\ K_2(n,k)\le Cn(k+1)^a\}.\] Here \(K_2(n,k)\) is the largest number of distinct \(k\)-point subsets strictly separable by a line in an \(n\)-point planar set with no three collinear points. Its full definition is below. The bound must be uniform in both integer parameters. Logarithmic factors and exact extremal counts are not requested.
cards.definitions:
For a finite set \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^2\), let
\[
\mathcal S_k(P)=\bigl\{S\subseteq P:\ |S|=k,\ 
\exists(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}\ 
\exists t\in\mathbb R:\ 
a x+b y<t\ \forall(x,y)\in S,\ 
a x+b y>t\ \forall(x,y)\in P\setminus S\bigr\}.
\]
For integers \(n\ge2\) and \(1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), define
\[
K_2(n,k)=
\max_{\substack{P\subseteq\mathbb R^2,\ |P|=n\\
                 \text{no three points of }P\text{ are collinear}}}
|\mathcal S_k(P)|.
\]


The plane \(\mathbb R^2\) has arbitrary real coordinates. A point set contains distinct points. General position here means exactly that no three points lie on one affine line; there is no grid, precision, distribution or convex-position restriction.

The affine line \(a x+b y=t\) has nonzero normal vector \((a,b)\). The strict inequalities in the definition place all points of \(S\) on one side and all other points on the opposite side. In particular the separating line contains no input point. A member of \(\mathcal S_k(P)\) is a k-set. Each subset is counted once, regardless of how many lines separate it.

The maximum is well-defined: every count is an integer between zero and \(\binom nk\), and there are general-position point sets of each permitted size. Thus the set of attained counts is a nonempty finite set of integers even though coordinates range over infinitely many possibilities.

Complementing subsets gives the same count for \(k\) and \(n-k\). Sizes zero and \(n\) each give one subset, so the stated domain captures the nontrivial range. The target is a combinatorial extremal function, not the time complexity of listing k-sets.

In the context, a directed j-edge joins two input points and has exactly \(j\) other points strictly to its left. For even \(n\), an undirected halving edge has \((n-2)/2\) other points on each side of its supporting line. The line through this edge is not a strict separator, since it passes through two points. The requested exponent is \[x_{\mathrm{kset}}=\inf\{a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:\exists C>0\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall 1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\ K_2(n,k)\le C n(k+1)^a\}.\] The integer parameter domain is the same as above. The coefficient \(C\) may depend on \(a\), but not on either parameter or the point configuration. The cited upper bound ensures \(0\le x_{\mathrm{kset}}\le1/3\). The infimum need not be attained. Thus a value zero permits subpolynomial dependence on \(k\) and does not assert a linear bound \(O(n)\). This records the exponent of the dependence on subset size after factoring out the linear dependence on the number of points; it does not assert a two-sided power-law asymptotic.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply \(a\) and prove \(|a-x_{\mathrm{kset}}|\le1/100\) in Lean. For each feasible exponent, one coefficient \(C\) must work for every legal pair \((n,k)\). To exclude an exponent, show that every proposed \(C>0\) fails at some such pair. The infimum need not be attained. A [certified enclosing interval](definitions.html#numerical-answers) of width at most \(1/50\) also suffices via its midpoint.

Its persistent gap tests the strength of crossing-number methods and geometric constructions, with consequences for output-sensitive and parametric algorithms.

context_blocks.text: A linear cut realizes only a restricted collection of subsets of a point set. Fixing the subset size measures this restriction more precisely than counting all possible cuts together. For \(k=1\), the separable points are precisely the vertices of the convex hull, the smallest convex set containing \(P\). Their maximum number is \(n\). The unresolved part concerns how the count grows when the selected subset size grows too.

Point-line duality relates these counts to levels in arrangements of lines. A level follows the positions with a prescribed number of arrangement lines below them. Dey’s general upper bound is \(O(nk^{1/3})\) on the domain of this card. Tóth’s constructions give \(n\exp(\Omega(\sqrt{\log k}))\) k-sets. Thus the existing upper and lower estimates do not differ by only a universal constant when \(k\) increases.

Consequently \(K_2(n,n/2)\) is twice the maximum number of halving edges. The index \((n-2)/2\) counts points on one side of a halving edge, not the size of a halving subset.

Nivasch’s construction gives \(\Omega\!\left(n\exp(\sqrt{\ln4}\sqrt{\ln n})/\sqrt{\ln n}\right)\) halving edges for every even \(n\), with an asymptotically larger exponent constant than earlier constructions. Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm. This lower-bound expression grows faster than \(n(\log n)^A\) for every fixed \(A\), but slower than \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). These comparisons concern the displayed construction, not a proved upper bound on the unknown optimum.

The 2024 halving-line paper improves lower-order and finite-size terms while retaining the leading four-thirds upper power in the balanced case. Such lower-order changes do not themselves determine the uniform exponent selected here.

Nivasch’s construction gives \(\Omega\!\left(n\exp(\sqrt{\ln4}\sqrt{\ln n})/\sqrt{\ln n}\right)\) halving edges for every even \(n\), with an asymptotically larger exponent constant than earlier constructions. Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm. This lower-bound expression grows faster than \(n(\log n)^A\) for every fixed \(A\), but slower than \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). These comparisons concern the displayed construction, not a proved upper bound on the unknown optimum.

The 2024 halving-line paper improves lower-order and finite-size terms while retaining the leading four-thirds upper power in the balanced case. Such lower-order changes do not themselves determine the uniform exponent selected here.

cards.title: Minimax sample complexity of proper agnostic online reinforcement learning
cards.formal:
For proper agnostic online reinforcement learning in the finite episodic model below, determine \(N(\Pi,H,\varepsilon)+1\) up to universal constant factors. Supply one function \(g\) of the given policy tables, layers, start state, horizon and accuracy, and constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) such that
\[c\,g(\Pi,H,\varepsilon)\le N(\Pi,H,\varepsilon)+1\le C\,g(\Pi,H,\varepsilon)\]
for every legal finite instance description and every real \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\). Here \(N\) is the minimax number of training episodes. This is the TCS500 benchmark’s quantitative finite-state version of the source question.
cards.definitions:
An instance description specifies a horizon \(H\ge1\), finite nonempty disjoint state layers \(S_1,\ldots,S_H\), a designated initial state \(s_0\) in \(S_1\), a fixed action set {0,1}, and a nonempty finite class \(\Pi\) of deterministic policies. A policy is a table assigning one action to every state; the layer identifies time. The learner receives all these tables. The unknown MDP has arbitrary stochastic transitions from layer h to h+1, and a terminal reward in [0,1] whose distribution depends on the last state and action. Earlier rewards are zero. All probability distributions may have arbitrary real probabilities. The value \(V(\pi)\) is expected terminal reward from \(s_0\).

Each episode starts afresh at \(s_0\) and follows the actual transitions for H steps. The learner observes visited states, chosen actions and the terminal reward. During training it may choose arbitrary randomized actions based on the entire history, including previous episodes. It cannot reset to an intermediate state, sample a chosen transition or inspect the transition/reward tables. There is no computation or policy-evaluation cost restriction: this is statistical complexity with measurable randomized learning rules.

\(N(\Pi,H,\varepsilon)\) is the least nonnegative integer N for which some such rule, after at most N complete episodes, outputs a member \(\hat\pi\) of \(\Pi\) with \(V(\hat\pi)\ge\max_{\pi\in\Pi}V(\pi)-\varepsilon\) with probability at least 2/3, for every MDP on these layers. The layer sets and start state are understood as part of \(\Pi\)’s description. N is finite, since testing every policy separately is allowed.

The required answer supplies an explicit expression or structural parameter g of the policy tables, layers, H and \(\varepsilon\), and universal constants c,C>0 with \(cg\le N+1\le Cg\) for every description. A definition merely repeating the optimization over learners and MDPs is not a determination. The added one handles classes learnable without samples. This narrows the broad characterization request to a specified minimax quantity; dependence on state count is not prohibited in the expression. It fixes proper output, binary actions and terminal rewards rather than silently treating all online RL models as equivalent.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked characterization by one explicitly described \(g\), with matching bounds for \(N+1\) and constants independent of the full instance and accuracy. A singleton policy class has \(N=0\), so the bounds must cover \(N+1=1\) there. Prove the upper bound using episodic online access and a policy in the given class. Prove the lower bound for every allowed learner. The local definitions specify which structural characterizations qualify.

cards.title: Area law for gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians
cards.formal: For every choice of integers \(q\ge2\), \(r,g\ge1\) and real numbers \(J,\Delta>0\), does there exist a finite constant \(C=C(q,r,g,J,\Delta)\ge0\) with the following property? For every square-lattice size \(L\ge1\), every Hamiltonian satisfying the locality, norm, incidence, unique-ground-state and global-gap conditions below, and every subset \(A\subseteq\Lambda_L\), its ground state satisfies \[S(\rho_A)\le C\,|\partial A|.\] The constant must be independent of \(L\), the region and the particular interaction matrices. This is an entropy area law for general uniformly gapped two-dimensional local systems.
cards.definitions:
Let \(\Lambda_L=\{1,\ldots,L\}^2\), with open boundaries and a copy of \(\mathbb C^q\) at each site. The full Hilbert space is \(\mathcal H_L=\bigotimes_{x\in\Lambda_L}\mathbb C^q\), with the standard product basis and inner product \(\langle u,v\rangle=u^\dagger v\). Dagger denotes conjugate transpose. A Hamiltonian is a Hermitian operator \(H=\sum_a h_a\), with a finite list of Hermitian interaction terms. Each term acts as identity outside a specified nonempty support \(X_a\subseteq\Lambda_L\). Its support has diameter at most \(r\) in the maximum-coordinate distance \(d_\infty(x,y)=\max\{|x_1-y_1|,|x_2-y_2|\}\). A one-site support has diameter zero. Each site belongs to at most \(g\) listed supports; terms with equal supports are counted separately. Every term has operator norm at most \(J\), where \(\|T\|=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\|Tv\|\) and \(\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}\). The terms need not be positive, commute, be translation invariant or admit a common energy-minimizing state.

List the eigenvalues of \(H\), with multiplicity, as \(E_0\le E_1\le\cdots\). Its lowest eigenspace is required to have dimension one and \(E_1-E_0\ge\Delta\). Choose a unit eigenvector \(\psi\) for \(E_0\). Uniqueness means uniqueness up to global phase, so \(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\) is uniquely specified. The gap condition concerns the entire Hamiltonian only. No lower gap bound is assumed for subregions or subsets of its interaction terms. Both \(J\) and \(\Delta\) are in the same fixed energy units.

For \(A\subseteq\Lambda_L\), let \(A^c=\Lambda_L\setminus A\) and let \(\rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_{A^c}(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\). Partial trace is defined in product-basis indices by \[(\rho_A)_{u,v}=\sum_z\psi_{(u,z)}\,\overline{\psi_{(v,z)}},\] where \(u,v\) index basis configurations on \(A\), \(z\) ranges over configurations on \(A^c\), and tuples are placed in the original site order. This is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix of trace one. If its eigenvalues are \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_D\), its entropy in bits is \(S(\rho_A)=-\sum_{j=1}^D\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\).

The geometric boundary \(\partial A\) consists of unordered nearest-neighbor lattice edges \(\{x,y\}\) with exactly one endpoint in \(A\), where \(|x_1-y_1|+|x_2-y_2|=1\). Its cardinality is measured in lattice units and is defined by geometry, even if a particular Hamiltonian has no term crossing an edge. No exterior vertices or periodic wrap-around edges are added. Regions may be disconnected or touch the exterior boundary. Empty and full regions have zero entropy and zero internal boundary. The interaction matrices may have arbitrary complex entries and may vary with location and with \(L\). There is no finite input encoding, state-preparation task, efficient computation requirement or frustration-free assumption. The question asks for a uniform mathematical entropy bound across all the specified finite systems.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal statement with the displayed order of quantifiers, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A negative answer fixes one choice of \(q,r,g,J,\Delta\) and shows that for every finite \(C\ge0\), there is an admissible system and region violating the bound. Equivalently, it may exhibit a sequence with these same fixed local parameters, unique ground states, gaps at least \(\Delta\), and unbounded ratios \(S(\rho_A)/|\partial A|\) on nontrivial regions. Allowing the gap to close, the interaction norm or local dimension to grow, or the lowest eigenspace to become degenerate does not refute this statement. A positive result for frustration-free or locally gapped systems, only one family of interactions, or an entropy bound with an unbounded extra logarithmic or subpolynomial factor does not prove it. No algorithm for finding the ground state is required. The statement is an exact yes/no bound; a fixed additive approximation to individual entropies is not a substitute.

context_blocks.text: A region containing \(m\) sites has entropy at most \(m\log_2q\). For a square block with side length \(\ell\), this volume bound is quadratic in \(\ell\), while the conjecture permits only a constant times its boundary length. Fixing both interaction norms and the gap prevents rescaling an increasingly gapless family from appearing uniformly gapped.

Hastings proves the corresponding entropy bound for gapped one-dimensional local systems. An interval has only a constant number of boundary edges, so its entropy stays bounded as the chain grows. Grouping columns of a two-dimensional lattice into single one-dimensional sites does not give a constant independent of width: each grouped site has dimension \(q^L\).

Anshu, Arad, and Gosset make major progress for frustration-free systems with a local gap. Frustration freeness means one state minimizes every local term; the local-gap assumption controls Hamiltonians obtained from subsets of terms, and is stronger than the global gap here. Their cited version proves a vertical-cut entropy bound \(n^{1+O((\log  n)^{- 1/5})}\) for cut length n. It is asymptotically almost linear, but the remaining factor is not a constant and neither extra assumption follows from the statement in this card.

Anshu, Harrow, and Soleimanifar prove an area law for entanglement spread, a measure of variation among the Schmidt coefficients after an appropriate smoothing. This controls a different feature of entanglement from its entropy. For intuition, a maximally entangled state can have arbitrarily many equal Schmidt coefficients: its spread is zero while its entropy is the logarithm of their number. A spread bound therefore does not by itself answer the entropy question.

Arad, Firanko, and Jain’s February 2026 theorem treats mutual information of the maximally mixed ground state. It assumes a sufficiently accurate approximation to the ground-space projector whose operator Schmidt rank is suitably small. Constructing such an approximation for general gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians remains a missing ingredient; the general wording of the title does not remove this hypothesis.

Garratt and Abanin’s April 2026 preprint provides thermodynamic upper bounds and proves area laws for frustration-free systems when ground-space degeneracies of the relevant subsystem Hamiltonians have suitable boundary scaling. A unique ground state for the full system does not impose that condition on each subsystem. These results retain additional assumptions.

The computational significance also needs care. Huang proves that two-dimensional local Hamiltonian instances whose ground states satisfy area laws can still be QMA-complete. Those instances are not claimed to have the uniform gap fixed here. The result nevertheless shows why an entropy bound alone should not be advertised as a general efficient classical algorithm for finding or manipulating two-dimensional ground states.

cards.title: Quantum capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel
cards.formal: Determine the unassisted quantum-capacity function \(Q(q)=Q(\mathcal D_q)\) for every real \(q\in[0,1]\), where the qubit depolarizing channel is \[\mathcal D_q(\rho)=(1-q)\rho+\frac q3(X\rho X+Y\rho Y+Z\rho Z).\] The parameter \(q\) is the total probability of a nonidentity Pauli error. Capacity uses the operational definition below and is measured in qubits per independent channel use. The quantitative benchmark accepts a function with absolute error at most \(1/100\) throughout the whole domain.
cards.definitions:
For the standard basis \(|0\rangle,|1\rangle\) of \(\mathbb C^2\), define \(X|0\rangle=|1\rangle\), \(X|1\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(Z|0\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(Z|1\rangle=-|1\rangle\), and \(Y=iXZ\), where \(i^2=-1\). Each of the three nonidentity errors has probability \(q/3\), and identity has probability \(1-q\). The formula therefore defines a channel for every real \(q\in[0,1]\). On general matrices it extends complex-linearly. In the coding definition, take \(A=B=\mathbb C^2\) and \(\Phi=\mathcal D_q\). The parameter is fixed across a code block and across the sequence of block lengths; a different parameter may have a different code sequence.

A density matrix on \(\mathbb C^d\) is a Hermitian matrix \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\) satisfying \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1\). Dagger denotes conjugate transpose and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. A quantum channel from \(\mathbb C^a\) to \(\mathbb C^b\) is a complex-linear map on matrices of the form \(\Psi(X)=\sum_j K_jXK_j^\dagger\), with finitely many \(b\)-by-\(a\) matrices obeying \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I_a\). These are precisely the completely positive trace-preserving maps, abbreviated CPTP. Matrices in coding operations may have arbitrary complex entries. Memorylessness means that \(n\) uses of a fixed channel \(\Phi:A\to B\) act as the tensor power \(\Phi^{\otimes n}\), with independent noise and the same channel on every use.

For each integer \(n\ge1\), a code consists of a nonnegative integer \(k_n\), a CPTP encoder \(E_n\) from \(k_n\) qubits to \(A^{\otimes n}\), and a CPTP decoder \(D_n\) from \(B^{\otimes n}\) to \(k_n\) qubits. A qubit is a copy of \(\mathbb C^2\), so the message space has dimension \(2^{k_n}\). Let \[|\Omega_k\rangle=2^{-k/2}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^k}|x\rangle_R\otimes|x\rangle_M\] be a maximally entangled unit vector between an untouched reference register \(R\) and a message register \(M\), each of dimension \(2^k\). For \(k=0\), both spaces are one-dimensional and the sum has one term. The entanglement fidelity of a code is \[F_n=\langle\Omega_{k_n}|\bigl[\operatorname{id}_R\otimes(D_n\circ\Phi^{\otimes n}\circ E_n)\bigr](|\Omega_{k_n}\rangle\langle\Omega_{k_n}|)|\Omega_{k_n}\rangle.\] The identity map leaves the reference unchanged, and \(\circ\) denotes composition, with the rightmost operation applied first. This tests preservation of quantum information and its correlations, rather than only classical basis labels.

A real rate \(r\ge0\) is achievable if there is a sequence of these codes, one for every \(n\ge1\), such that \(F_n\to1\) and \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}k_n/n\ge r\). Define \(Q(\Phi)\) as the supremum of achievable rates, in qubits per channel use. Rate zero is always achievable. The encoder and decoder may jointly process their entire blocks, use local ancillary systems and discard local systems. There is no bound on their computation or circuit sizes and no uniformity requirement on the sequence of codes. They depend on the channel but not on the unknown input message state. No preshared entanglement, additional classical communication, feedback or auxiliary quantum channel is supplied. Despite this short channel description, its quantum transmission limit allows arbitrary collective encodings over arbitrarily long blocks. The entanglement-fidelity criterion keeps the distinction between transmitting an unknown quantum state and sending only classical data.

Parameter conventions matter: the probabilities \((1-3p,p,p,p)\) correspond to \(p=q/3\). The expression \((1-\lambda)\rho+\lambda I/2\) has \(\lambda=4q/3\), with the usual convex-mixture interpretation only for \(q\le3/4\). Thus \(q=3/4\) is the completely depolarizing channel; \(q=1\) still specifies a valid channel, but is a different map. All thresholds here use total Pauli error \(q\).

The quantum coding theorem identifies the operational capacity with \(\sup_{n\ge1} n^{-1}\max_\rho I_c(\rho,\Phi^{\otimes n})\). Here \(\rho\) ranges over all input density matrices on \(A^{\otimes n}\). If \(|\psi\rangle\) is a purification of \(\rho\), meaning a unit vector on a reference and the input with input marginal \(\rho\), and \(\omega=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Phi^{\otimes n})(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\), then \(I_c=S(\omega_{B^{\otimes n}})-S(\omega)\). The marginal is obtained by tracing out the reference. For eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\) of a density matrix, \(S=-\sum_j\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\). The result is independent of the chosen purification. This exact regularized expression includes every block length; it is not an evaluation of the capacity curve or a finite stopping rule.

A known lower bound is \(\max\{0,1-h_2(q)-q\log_2 3\}\), where \(h_2(q)=-q\log_2q-(1-q)\log_2(1-q)\), with the endpoint convention \(0\log_2 0=0\). Its positive part vanishes near \(q=0.1893\). cards.title: Computability of quantum channel capacity
cards.formal: Does there exist a single deterministic classical Turing algorithm that, for every valid finite description of a memoryless finite-dimensional quantum channel \(\Phi\) specified below and every positive rational \(\varepsilon\), halts and outputs a rational \(r\) satisfying \(|r-Q(\Phi)|\le\varepsilon\)? Here \(Q\) is unassisted, vanishing-error quantum capacity in qubits per channel use. The algorithm must work for all valid descriptions and all positive requested accuracies; there is no time or space bound beyond eventual halting.
cards.definitions:
The input consists of positive integers \(d_A,d_B\), a finite program \(P\) for an ordinary deterministic Turing machine, and a positive rational \(\varepsilon\). Integers use binary notation and a rational uses a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. Programs use one fixed effective encoding over a finite alphabet; choosing a different standard encoding only changes effective translations. Write \(A=\mathbb C^{d_A}\), \(B=\mathbb C^{d_B}\). The program \(P\), on every positive integer input \(m\), is promised to halt and output a complex matrix \(J_m\) of order \(d_Ad_B\), with rational real and imaginary entries in this encoding. There is a matrix \(J\) such that, for every entry, both its real and imaginary parts differ from those of \(J_m\) by at most \(2^{-m}\). No additional time bound on \(P\) is promised. The approximating matrices themselves need not be positive or trace preserving.

Index matrix entries by pairs \((i,u)\), with \(1\le i\le d_A\) and \(1\le u\le d_B\). The limiting matrix is promised to be positive semidefinite and to satisfy \[\sum_{u=1}^{d_B}J_{(i,u),(j,u)}=\delta_{ij}\qquad(1\le i,j\le d_A),\] where \(\delta_{ij}\) is one if \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. These conditions say \(\operatorname{Tr}_B J=I_A\). They make \(J\) the unnormalized Choi matrix of the unique CPTP channel defined on matrix units by \([\Phi(|i\rangle\langle j|)]_{u,v}=J_{(i,u),(j,v)}\) and extended complex-linearly. Equivalently, \(J=\sum_{i,j}|i\rangle\langle j|\otimes\Phi(|i\rangle\langle j|)\). The guarantee supplies effective approximation of arbitrary computable complex entries; algebraic-entry channels and ordinary finite circuits over computable gates are included. The algorithm receives the program's finite code and may execute it. It receives no oracle deciding equality, positivity or ordering of arbitrary computable real numbers.

All guarantees for the requested capacity algorithm apply only to inputs satisfying these promises. It need not recognize validity and has no prescribed behavior on invalid descriptions. Every valid program describing the same channel must yield an approximation to that channel's same capacity, though the output rational and running time may differ between programs. The description specifies the channel, not a particular encoder or decoder.

A density matrix on \(\mathbb C^d\) is a Hermitian matrix \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\) satisfying \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1\). Dagger denotes conjugate transpose and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. A quantum channel from \(\mathbb C^a\) to \(\mathbb C^b\) is a complex-linear map on matrices of the form \(\Psi(X)=\sum_j K_jXK_j^\dagger\), with finitely many \(b\)-by-\(a\) matrices obeying \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I_a\). These are precisely the completely positive trace-preserving maps, abbreviated CPTP. Matrices in coding operations may have arbitrary complex entries. Memorylessness means that \(n\) uses of a fixed channel \(\Phi:A\to B\) act as the tensor power \(\Phi^{\otimes n}\), with independent noise and the same channel on every use.

For each integer \(n\ge1\), a code consists of a nonnegative integer \(k_n\), a CPTP encoder \(E_n\) from \(k_n\) qubits to \(A^{\otimes n}\), and a CPTP decoder \(D_n\) from \(B^{\otimes n}\) to \(k_n\) qubits. A qubit is a copy of \(\mathbb C^2\), so the message space has dimension \(2^{k_n}\). Let \[|\Omega_k\rangle=2^{-k/2}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^k}|x\rangle_R\otimes|x\rangle_M\] be a maximally entangled unit vector between an untouched reference register \(R\) and a message register \(M\), each of dimension \(2^k\). For \(k=0\), both spaces are one-dimensional and the sum has one term. The entanglement fidelity of a code is \[F_n=\langle\Omega_{k_n}|\bigl[\operatorname{id}_R\otimes(D_n\circ\Phi^{\otimes n}\circ E_n)\bigr](|\Omega_{k_n}\rangle\langle\Omega_{k_n}|)|\Omega_{k_n}\rangle.\] The identity map leaves the reference unchanged, and \(\circ\) denotes composition, with the rightmost operation applied first. This tests preservation of quantum information and its correlations, rather than only classical basis labels.

A real rate \(r\ge0\) is achievable if there is a sequence of these codes, one for every \(n\ge1\), such that \(F_n\to1\) and \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}k_n/n\ge r\). Define \(Q(\Phi)\) as the supremum of achievable rates, in qubits per channel use. Rate zero is always achievable. The encoder and decoder may jointly process their entire blocks, use local ancillary systems and discard local systems. There is no bound on their computation or circuit sizes and no uniformity requirement on the sequence of codes. They depend on the channel but not on the unknown input message state. No preshared entanglement, additional classical communication, feedback or auxiliary quantum channel is supplied. context_blocks.text: Capacity is the best rate at which a noisy channel can transmit information reliably after coding over many uses. For quantum transmission, the object being preserved is an arbitrary quantum state, including its entanglement with a reference system. A channel may badly corrupt each individual input and still support a positive asymptotic rate through suitable coding. This card asks whether that optimal rate can always be computed to requested precision at all.

The quantum coding theorem identifies the operational capacity with \(\sup_{n\ge1} n^{-1}\max_\rho I_c(\rho,\Phi^{\otimes n})\). Here \(\rho\) ranges over all input density matrices on \(A^{\otimes n}\). If \(|\psi\rangle\) is a purification of \(\rho\), meaning a unit vector on a reference and the input with input marginal \(\rho\), and \(\omega=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Phi^{\otimes n})(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\), then \(I_c=S(\omega_{B^{\otimes n}})-S(\omega)\). The marginal is obtained by tracing out the reference. For eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\) of a density matrix, \(S=-\sum_j\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\). The result is independent of the chosen purification. This exact regularized expression includes every block length; it is not an evaluation of the capacity curve or a finite stopping rule.

The regularized formula gives approximable finite-dimensional objectives at every fixed block length. This yields lower semicomputability: certified rational lower bounds can approach capacity. Such a sequence alone need not tell an algorithm when its distance from the limit is below a requested tolerance.

Cubitt and coauthors prove that no fixed number of channel uses suffices uniformly over all channels even to detect positive coherent information. For every chosen block length, they construct a channel whose optimized coherent information is zero there but whose capacity is positive. The channel can change with the chosen length. This does not rule out an algorithm with stopping time depending on the channel description and requested accuracy.

The input convention is important because a quantum channel is described by real and complex numbers. A finite program that supplies certified rational approximations gives an algorithm meaningful access to those numbers without granting exact tests of arbitrary computable-real equality. It also includes ordinary finite circuit descriptions over computable gates. The validity of the channel and approximation program is promised; solving the separate problem of recognizing all valid descriptions is not required.

Leung and Smith prove continuity of unassisted quantum capacity in finite output dimension, with an explicit bound in terms of channel distance and dimension. Thus small errors in specifying a fixed-dimensional channel change its capacity by a controlled amount. This prevents a simple discontinuity argument from settling this approximation question. Continuity controls perturbations of the channel, while the missing stopping rule concerns convergence over code block lengths.

The 2025 review Undecidability in Physics distinguishes this question from established undecidability results for other information-theoretic quantities. Channels with memory can carry an evolving hidden state across uses; that is different from repeating \(\Phi\) independently. Zero-error capacities demand perfect distinguishability at finite stages, unlike an error that tends to zero under asymptotic coding. Neither change can be imported silently into the present problem.

Bhattacharyya, Mehta and Zhao prove in 2026 that approximating quantum capacity is QMA-hard for channels specified succinctly by circuits. Their promise distinguishes capacity at least \(3/4\) from capacity at most \(1/4\), even for degradable channels. This is strong evidence against efficient computation, but it leaves unrestricted computability untouched: a QMA-hard problem can still have an exhaustive terminating algorithm. Circuit size also differs substantially from the length of a fully expanded channel matrix.

Their corrected March 2026 version proves undecidability for a separate restricted capacity: one-shot, entanglement-assisted, zero-error classical communication through a classical-to-quantum channel, with maximally entangled assistance and projective decoding measurements. Those restrictions are part of the theorem. The paper explicitly says it does not resolve general quantum-capacity computability. Its revision history records a correction to the earlier treatment of the assisted zero-error result.

It is also necessary to separate approximation from deciding whether the answer is exactly zero. Even when a nonnegative real quantity is computable to arbitrary error, every finite approximation can leave open whether it is zero or merely very small. cards.context:
Capacity is the best rate at which a noisy channel can transmit information reliably after coding over many uses. For quantum transmission, the object being preserved is an arbitrary quantum state, including its entanglement with a reference system. A channel may badly corrupt each individual input and still support a positive asymptotic rate through suitable coding. This card asks whether that optimal rate can always be computed to requested precision at all.

The quantum coding theorem identifies the operational capacity with \(\sup_{n\ge1} n^{-1}\max_\rho I_c(\rho,\Phi^{\otimes n})\). Here \(\rho\) ranges over all input density matrices on \(A^{\otimes n}\). If \(|\psi\rangle\) is a purification of \(\rho\), meaning a unit vector on a reference and the input with input marginal \(\rho\), and \(\omega=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Phi^{\otimes n})(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\), then \(I_c=S(\omega_{B^{\otimes n}})-S(\omega)\). The marginal is obtained by tracing out the reference. For eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\) of a density matrix, \(S=-\sum_j\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\). The result is independent of the chosen purification. This exact regularized expression includes every block length; it is not an evaluation of the capacity curve or a finite stopping rule.

The regularized formula gives approximable finite-dimensional objectives at every fixed block length. This yields lower semicomputability: certified rational lower bounds can approach capacity. Such a sequence alone need not tell an algorithm when its distance from the limit is below a requested tolerance.

Cubitt and coauthors prove that no fixed number of channel uses suffices uniformly over all channels even to detect positive coherent information. For every chosen block length, they construct a channel whose optimized coherent information is zero there but whose capacity is positive. The channel can change with the chosen length. This does not rule out an algorithm with stopping time depending on the channel description and requested accuracy.

The input convention is important because a quantum channel is described by real and complex numbers. A finite program that supplies certified rational approximations gives an algorithm meaningful access to those numbers without granting exact tests of arbitrary computable-real equality. It also includes ordinary finite circuit descriptions over computable gates. The validity of the channel and approximation program is promised; solving the separate problem of recognizing all valid descriptions is not required.

Leung and Smith prove continuity of unassisted quantum capacity in finite output dimension, with an explicit bound in terms of channel distance and dimension. Thus small errors in specifying a fixed-dimensional channel change its capacity by a controlled amount. This prevents a simple discontinuity argument from settling this approximation question. Continuity controls perturbations of the channel, while the missing stopping rule concerns convergence over code block lengths.

The 2025 review Undecidability in Physics distinguishes this question from established undecidability results for other information-theoretic quantities. Channels with memory can carry an evolving hidden state across uses; that is different from repeating \(\Phi\) independently. Circuit size also differs substantially from the length of a fully expanded channel matrix.

cards.definitions:
The security parameter is an integer \(\lambda\ge1\), supplied as the unary string \(1^\lambda\). A negligible function is a map \(\nu:\mathbb N_{>0}\to[0,1]\) such that, for every integer \(c\ge1\), eventually \(\nu(\lambda)\le\lambda^{-c}\). Each security quantifier may have its own negligible function. Polynomial bounds have fixed constants and exponents independent of \(\lambda\).

An \(m\)-qubit state is a positive semidefinite complex matrix of trace one on \((\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes m}\). Algorithms use quantum circuits over the fixed gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), preparation of zero qubits, computational-basis measurement, classical control and discarding qubits. Here \(H=2^{-1/2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), and \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\). Classical inputs and outputs are bit strings. All gate applications, classical computation and input/output operations are charged. A uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithm has one deterministic classical polynomial-time circuit generator, and its circuit size and classical control time are polynomial in the input length on every branch. Honest algorithms receive no advice. Their security-parameter-dependent lengths are positive, polynomially bounded and polynomial-time computable.

An adversary is any family of polynomial-size circuits in this model, with arbitrary polynomial-size classical descriptions depending on \(\lambda\). Equivalently it may use polynomially many classical advice bits depending only on \(\lambda\), independently of the sampled secret or challenge bit. It may prepare quantum work registers from zero but receives no arbitrary quantum advice. There is no oracle or uncharged computation. The descriptions of all honest algorithms are public.

An EFI pair consists of one uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithm \(G\) with output \(m(\lambda)\) qubits. Write \(\rho_{b,\lambda}\) for the mixed output of \(G(1^\lambda,b)\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\). The following two requirements hold:
\[
\exists p\ \exists\lambda_0\ \forall\lambda\ge\lambda_0:
\quad \frac12\|\rho_{0,\lambda}-\rho_{1,\lambda}\|_1\ge\frac1{p(\lambda)},
\]
where \(p\) is a positive polynomial, and, for every adversary \(D\), its distinguishing advantage
\[
\left|\Pr[D(1^\lambda,\rho_{0,\lambda})=1]
-\Pr[D(1^\lambda,\rho_{1,\lambda})=1]\right|
\]
is negligible. The trace norm is \(\|X\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{X^\dagger X}\). The distinguishing experiment supplies one challenge state. Its preparation randomness and all measurements are included in the probabilities.

An efficiently verifiable one-way state generator consists of three uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithms \(\mathrm{KeyGen},\mathrm{StateGen},\mathrm{Ver}\). The first, on \(1^\lambda\), samples a classical key \(k\in\{0,1\}^{\kappa(\lambda)}\). The second, on \((1^\lambda,k)\), outputs an \(m(\lambda)\)-qubit state \(\sigma_{k,\lambda}\), which may be mixed. The third, on \((1^\lambda,k',\sigma)\), outputs an acceptance bit; a key of the wrong length is rejected. Correctness requires
\[
\Pr_{k\leftarrow\mathrm{KeyGen}(1^\lambda)}
 [\mathrm{Ver}(1^\lambda,k,\sigma_{k,\lambda})=1]\ge1-\nu(\lambda)
\]
for some negligible \(\nu\). This is averaged over the generated key, not a promise of correctness for every bit string.

Security requires that, for every positive integer-valued polynomial copy bound \(t(\lambda)\) and every adversary \(A\), the following success probability is negligible:
\[
\Pr\!\left[
\mathrm{Ver}(1^\lambda,k',\sigma_{k,\lambda})=1:
\ k\leftarrow\mathrm{KeyGen}(1^\lambda),\
 k'\leftarrow A(1^\lambda,\sigma_{k,\lambda}^{\otimes t(\lambda)})
\right].
\]
Conditioned on \(k\), all copies are produced by independent runs of \(\mathrm{StateGen}\). The verifier's copy is fresh and independent of the copies supplied to \(A\). The probability includes key generation, state preparation and all measurements. The adversary wins by producing any accepted key, not necessarily the original key. In particular the verifier must be efficient; allowing it unlimited time defines a different primitive.

The proposition quantifies over existence of complete schemes, with their own polynomial lengths and running-time bounds. It does not prescribe a fixed transformation or loss of security from a given EFI generator. A counterexample relative to an added oracle, or impossibility for one restricted form of transformation, does not by itself negate this ordinary-model existence implication.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of this existence implication, or a complete Lean proof of its negation in the stated ordinary model. All correctness, polynomial-time and asymptotic security requirements must match the definitions, including efficient verification and classical rather than quantum advice. An equivalence with generators whose verifier has unlimited running time, an oracle-relative separation or a restriction on black-box constructions alone is insufficient.

cards.definitions:
For integers \(n\ge2\) and \(c\ge1\), let \(d=\lceil c\log_2 n\rceil\). An instance consists of two ordered lists \(A=(a^{(1)},\ldots,a^{(n)})\) and \(B=(b^{(1)},\ldots,b^{(n)})\) of vectors in \(\{0,1\}^d\). Repetitions, zero vectors and overlap between lists are allowed, with no promise on weights, intersections or number of solutions. Define ordinary integer inner products by
\[
\langle a,b\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_jb_j.
\]
The Orthogonal Vectors predicate is
\[
\mathrm{OV}(A,B)\iff\exists r\in[n]\ \exists s\in[n]:
\langle a^{(r)},b^{(s)}\rangle=0.
\]
The Hitting Set predicate is
\[
\mathrm{HS}(A,B)\iff\exists r\in[n]\ \forall s\in[n]:
\langle a^{(r)},b^{(s)}\rangle>0.
\]
Thus the hitting set must be one supplied vector from \(A\); this is not optimization over arbitrary subsets of a universe. The predicates are not each other’s negations. Both tasks output one decision bit and need not supply a witness.

Both models use explicit packed input: headers \(n,d\), then the two lists in their given order. A vector occupies \(\lceil d/w\rceil\) words, with coordinates from least to most significant bit and unused final bits zero. In the OV model a program fixes any integer \(\lambda\ge2\) and uses
\[
w_{\mathrm{OV}}=\lambda\lceil\log_2(n+d+2)\rceil.
\]
The HS model uses the completed HS card’s fixed eventual word size, with the finite-input correction needed to address the supplied input:
\[
w_{\mathrm{HS}}=
\max\!\left\{\lceil4\log_2(n+2)\rceil,
\lceil\log_2(2nd+n+d+8)\rceil\right\}.
\]
For every fixed \(c\), the second HS term is dominated by the first for all sufficiently large \(n\). It affects only a finite prefix and does not change the asymptotic hypothesis.

A program is finite and independent of \(n\). It has word registers and memory addressed by single words, with all non-input memory initially zero. An operation may read or write a constant number of addressed words, copy, compare, branch, add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\), take integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor, apply bitwise Boolean operations or shift. Shifts discard overflow and return zero for shift counts at least \(w\). In the HS model division or remainder by zero may return zero; OV programs must use nonzero divisors. A fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit random word costs one step. Compound multiword operations must be charged as their constituent operations. No arbitrary-precision or real arithmetic, input-dependent-width vector instruction, advice or oracle is available. The address universe is \(2^w\) words. Input access, preprocessing, lookup-table construction, randomness and output are all charged.

For \(P\in\{\mathrm{OV},\mathrm{HS}\}\), \(c\ge1\) and a real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), write \(\operatorname{Fast}_P(c,\varepsilon)\) if there exists a uniform randomized program in its respective model which halts on every allowed input and random tape, answers \(P\) correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) on each fixed input, and has constants \(K>0\) and integer \(n_0\ge2\) such that every execution on every input of every size \(n\ge n_0\) takes at most \(Kn^{2-\varepsilon}\) operations. Smaller inputs must also be decided with the stated error and finite runtime. The program, \(K,n_0\), and the OV word multiplier may depend on \(c,\varepsilon\), but not on \(n\). The bound is not merely expected time or average-input time. Deterministic programs are included by ignoring randomness.

Define
\[
\mathrm{OVH}_{\log}\iff
\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1)\ \exists c\ge1:
\neg\operatorname{Fast}_{\mathrm{OV}}(c,\varepsilon),
\]
\[
\mathrm{HSH}_{\log}\iff
\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1)\ \exists c\ge1:
\neg\operatorname{Fast}_{\mathrm{HS}}(c,\varepsilon),
\]
where \(c\) ranges over integers. Equivalently, failure of either hypothesis means that one positive saving works for every fixed \(c\), with separate programs allowed for different \(c\). No effective compiler producing these programs from \(c\), or one program handling all dimensions, is required.

The requested implication can therefore be written as
\[
\left[\exists\varepsilon\in(0,1)\ \forall c\ge1:
\operatorname{Fast}_{\mathrm{HS}}(c,\varepsilon)\right]
\Longrightarrow
\left[\exists\delta\in(0,1)\ \forall c\ge1:
\operatorname{Fast}_{\mathrm{OV}}(c,\delta)\right].
\]
The two savings need not be equal. This is an implication between the stated propositions; it does not impose an additional requirement of a black-box, deterministic, zero-error or any other particular reduction format. The source’s literal all-dimensions bound \(n^{2-\varepsilon}\operatorname{poly}(d)\) with one algorithm is a different uniformity convention and is not used here.

cards.title: Polynomial kernels for Directed Feedback Vertex Set
cards.formal:
Does Directed Feedback Vertex Set admit a deterministic polynomial kernel parameterized solely by the deletion budget? More precisely, do there exist a deterministic algorithm \(K\), constants \(C,c>0\), and a polynomial \(p\), such that for every finite digraph \(D\) and nonnegative integer \(k\), \(K\) runs in at most \(p(L)\) steps on the explicit input of bit length \(L\), and outputs one instance \((D^{\prime},k^{\prime})\) of the same problem satisfying
\[
D\text{ has a directed feedback vertex set of size at most }k
\iff
D^{\prime}\text{ has one of size at most }k^{\prime},
\]
with the entire output encoding having at most \(C(k+1)^{c}\) bits? The constants and algorithm must work for all inputs. No additional structural parameter or promise on the input or the remaining acyclic graph is permitted.
